title: [Chapitre] IX et IX bis. [Ateliers] : notes manuscrites (05-15/07/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
This is a scratch page written on the back of a typed Récoltes et Semailles page (the mirrored typescript about Mebkhout and Kashiwara shows through). It is unrelated to that text. The mathematics is a small finite order-theoretic or combinatorial experiment.

(1) The family. Take a 4-element index set I = {i, i', j, k}, written at the head of the formula as 'i,i'  j  k'. Grothendieck defines a family A of subsets E of I. A subset belongs to A if it does not separate i from i' (both i, i' ∈ E, or both ∉ E). In addition, the two extra subsets E = {i} and E = {i, j, k} are admitted; these two are labelled A' under the brace.
- The non-separating subsets are ∅, {j}, {k}, {j,k}, {i,i'}, {i,i',j}, {i,i',k}, I. They form a Boolean cube 2^3.
- Adding the two 'defects' gives 10 elements.
- This matches the 10 labelled vertices of the top-left drawing: 0, a', a, c, b', B, C, A, A', 1. That drawing is a perspective picture of a cube with additional vertices inserted, ordered by inclusion with arrows pointing upward.

(2) The hexagon. The hexagon below it has vertices A (top), b, C, a (bottom), B, c, with arrows on its edges. It is apparently the configuration being tested: three atoms-like elements and their pairwise joins arranged cyclically.

(3) The test. The bottom lines take the triple a', b, c with pairwise joins b'∨c = A, c∨a' = B, a'∨b = C. Under the three joins sit downward arrows to a, b, c, with verdicts 'pas OK!', 'OK', 'OK'. Grothendieck is checking whether certain elements lie below the relevant joins (an inclusion or covering condition of a hexagon or Desargues-type configuration). He finds that it fails for one of the three.

(4) Interpretation. The page reads as a search for a small counterexample in the theory of finite lattices or closure systems (posets of subsets, joins, a hexagonal configuration). A cube is deformed by adding two 'non-saturated' subsets to break the symmetry, and the configuration fails at one place.

The page gives no statement of the property being tested, and the top-right square sketch (a square subdivided into four) is unexplained. Without the neighbouring mathematical pages of the 1986 'Ateliers' notes, the exact goal cannot be determined.
errors: As ordered by inclusion, the 10-element family A is not a lattice. For example, {i} and {j} have two minimal upper bounds in A, {i,j,k} and {i,i',j}, so their join is not unique. If Grothendieck intended A to be a lattice with join ∨, then either ∨ means something other than the inclusion join or the family is not as transcribed. This may also be exactly the failure recorded by 'pas OK!'.
The notation 'P^3(I)' is unclear. It may denote subsets of I of a certain kind, or be a misreading of 𝔓(I); taken literally as an iterated power set, the definition does not parse.

ideas.what: A finite family of subsets of a 4-element set, consisting of the subsets not separating i from i' plus two extra subsets {i} and {i,j,k}, viewed as an ordered set (a deformed cube 2^3)
ideas.modern_name: Finite poset/lattice of subsets; closure system (Moore family) counterexample construction

ideas.what: Testing a hexagonal configuration: three elements with pairwise joins A, B, C, and whether each join dominates a given element (verdict OK / not OK)
ideas.modern_name: Checking a modularity/semimodularity or Desargues-type lattice condition on a small example

deep.surprise_reason: A routine scratch computation: a hand-built 10-element order of subsets of a 4-element set used to test a lattice-type configuration. It is too fragmentary to identify the property being tested, and it contains nothing that looks new.
transcription_corrections: Hexagon vertex labels are mixed case: A (top), b (upper right), C (right), a (bottom), B (lower left), and 'c' (lowercase, upper left) rather than a second 'C'.
'tel que' (abbreviated 'tq') is written under 'A' and is the start of the definition: 'A = { E ∈ 𝔓...(I) tel que ... }'.
The under-brace labels mark {i} and {i,j,k} as the two added elements, with 'A'' written under {i,j,k}.
In the last line the verdicts are 'pas OK!', 'OK', 'OK' under the arrows 'C↓a', 'C↓b', 'C↓c'; the first arrow has a crossed-out symbol.
The cube diagram labels include 'a'' near the bottom-left above 0, 'c' at the centre and 'b'' at the right, with A' at the top right next to 1.
